title: Why Did XOM, CVX, MPC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of energy companies Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM), Chevron Corp. (CVX), and Marathon Petroleum Corp. (MPC) surged to annual highs on Monday as oil prices rallied amid growing geopolitical tensions. Brent crude prices touched nearly $110 a barrel on Monday as tensions in the Middle East continued to ratchet up. A series of recent escalations, including attacks on commercial ships near the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine’s strike on a Russian refinery, stoked fears about a further constraint in fuel supplies, sending prices higher. Worries continued despite the U.S. government’s efforts to curtail rising prices, including planned fuel releases and changes to U.S. sanctions on Russian imported fuel. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, energy prices have been climbing steadily, boosting energy companies. As per Koyfin data, energy stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by a significant margin in 2026. Exxon Mobil, Chevron, and Marathon Petroleum shares surged to 52-week highs on Monday before closing lower amid the steep climb in oil prices. XOM stock hit an annual high of $179.30 during trading hours on Monday before closing about 0.4% down. CVX stock surged to a 52-week high of $225.67, but ended the session 0.28% lower. MPC stock rallied to a 52-week high of $493.98 during regular trading, but finished the day nearly 1% down. Retail sentiment around XOM, CVX and MPC stocks was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing on Stocktwits. XOM stock has gained more than 48% year-to-date, while CVX and MPC stocks have surged more than 47% and 200%, respectively. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Retail investors in Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) are floating multibillion-dollar buyout scenarios and steep share-price gains after CEO Angelos Stergiou marked the company’s 15th anniversary with a post about its “next chapter.” SLS stock jumped 5% on Monday to $10.49, snapping three straight losing sessions. In his LinkedIn post, Stergiou reflected on Sellas’ growth from a private startup into a public biotech advancing investigational cancer treatments GPS and SLS009. “Reaching 15 years isn't just about celebrating our history; it is about stepping into our next chapter with even greater focus, drive, and resolve,” he said. He acknowledged past setbacks and thanked shareholders, employees and trial participants, while reaffirming the company’s commitment to patients. “Our mission remains deeply personal, and our promise to the patients we aim to serve is steadfast. We look forward, God willing, to the best chapters that are still to be written with GPS and SLS009,” he added. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SLS slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid a 258% jump in 24-hour message volumes. One user said: “My opinion, Dr. Stergiou’s message was a master-class at reassuring EVERYONE that all is well.” A user also floated a minimum $40 billion valuation. Another user argued for a $50 billion valuation, calling a $247-per-share figure. A separate user proposed a $120 billion buyout scenario and also predicted a share price of $540-plus. Across bullish share-price predictions, including scenarios tied to clinical results, targets ranged from $100 to over $540. Discussing buyout news in case of favorable data, one user said: “If BO news post good data then there’s no stopping this beast (really no explanation required as it could go full berserker mode).” BO means buyout. Another user challenged the lofty valuations and said: “I will be so glad to get out of this ticker when it hits $15 again.” The CEO’s message comes as investors have been searching for potential deal signals in recent months. In June, a filing disclosed changes to executive severance arrangements, including lump-sum payment provisions for Stergiou. For CFO John Burns and chief development officer Dragan Cicic, qualifying departures within one month before or one year after a change of control would trigger 15 months of salary, the annual target bonus, up to 18 months of health-coverage reimbursements and full vesting of unvested equity. Sellas’ conference plans have provided another talking point. The company is listed at Booth 138, with a 20-by-30-foot space, for the Dec.12- Dec.15 American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. Major exhibitors include Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Merck, AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb. The booth size has fueled speculation about a partnership or acquisition. Currently, investors are awaiting data from Sellas’ two lead programs. The Phase 3 Regal trial is testing GPS, an immunotherapy targeting WT1, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients who achieved a second complete remission following salvage treatment. Its final-analysis process is triggered by 80 deaths. Sellas reported 78 events as of May 11. Reaching 80 precedes database lock, data review and analysis before results are disclosed. The company also expects fourth-quarter topline data from its 80-patient Phase 2 SLS009 study in newly diagnosed AML, including patients with early resistance to azacitidine and venetoclax. SLS009 is also being explored in pancreatic cancer. Preclinical findings from last month showed 17.9% apoptosis (programmed cell death) in a patient-derived tumor model resistant to Daraxonrasib, versus 2.8% with Daraxonrasib alone. Combining the drugs raised apoptosis to 36.5% and necrosis to 30.6%. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. U.S. stock futures climbed into positive territory late Monday as technology stocks rebounded after a sharp selloff last week. Meanwhile, markets are keenly watching the third-quarter (Q3) earnings season unfold, with about 70 S&P 500 companies slated to report earnings this week. As of 11:13 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.25%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.21% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.15%. On Monday, the three benchmark indexes closed mixed. The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding more than 290 points to close 1.11% higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.41% at close, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.07%. Technology and AI stocks were top of mind for markets on Monday as the sector reversed last week's steep selloff. Chip stocks led the climb on Monday. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) closed up nearly 2%, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) closed up 1.61%. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Micron Technology Inc. (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) all ended the session in green. The run comes ahead of vital Q3 results that will follow this week, which are likely to set the tone for the trajectory of technology shares. “Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration,” Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, said in a note, according to CNBC. Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, reportedly said in a note on Monday that the week will be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support, while noting that a hold is possible amid widespread, short-term oversold conditions. Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) are due to report Q3 results later this week, while multiple other semiconductor and technology companies, including Lam Research (LRCX) and Texas Instruments (TXN), will also post their results. AI-related power companies Bloom Energy (BE) and Valero Energy (VLO), along with big entertainment companies including Netflix Inc. (NFLX), will also announce their quarterly results. Meanwhile, rising oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainty have put downward pressure on markets. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $109.88 a barrel, up about 0.3%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $103.64 per barrel. Economist Peter Schiff said in a post on X, “Oil rose another 2.5% today. It's almost $104. If you think gas prices are high now, just wait until after the midterms when Trump has to turn off the spigots from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to keep it from running dry. Oil could hit $150, sending gas prices to record highs.” Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN): The company’s stock surged nearly 5% at close on Monday and continued to climb higher overnight after Morgan Stanley raised its price target and named it a ‘Top Pick.’ Cerebras Systems Inc. (CRWV): Shares of the neocloud company fell more than 1% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) all climbed overnight. Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.138%, and the 30-year Treasury yield was 5.473%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.09% amid ‘bullish’ sentiment. Asian markets opened lower on Tuesday, with South Korea's KOSPI, Japan’s Nikkei 225, China’s SSE Composite and Australian stocks all trading lower at the time of writing. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of Broadcom, Inc. (AVGO) reversed overnight losses to edge up 0.3% late Monday as a 10-year cloud agreement with NTT Docomo did little to ease retail skepticism, with traders seeking a recovery catalyst after CEO Hock Tan’s AI “casino” remarks. AVGO stock rose nearly 2% on Monday to close at $334.59, snapping three straight sessions of losses. Broadcom extended its 2019 deal with Docomo, in which the companies will align their long-term tech roadmaps to advance the private cloud underpinning the Japanese telecom operator’s digital services. The company called it Broadcom Japan’s first “comprehensive” 10-year agreement covering VMware software licenses, technical assistance and maintenance support. Financial terms were not disclosed. VMware Cloud Foundation will be at the core of the infrastructure. The deal targets three priorities: keeping services available during system upgrades, strengthening security and resilience, and accelerating the delivery of new services. Docomo will use the platform to expand capacity and manage traffic spikes, improve security patching and anomaly detection, and run virtual machines and containers on a common platform. Automation across development, testing and releases will help shorten the time needed to introduce new features. The companies also plan to expand AI-driven operations and prepare the infrastructure for future developments, including 6G and IOWN. The agreement comes a week after Tan’s comments at a Singapore panel, where he called capital the biggest constraint on further AI development as Broadcom works through wafer and memory shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling,” Tan said when asked about cheaper AI models, Reuters noted. His remarks addressed investment into the broader AI sector. Tan also acknowledged that Anthropic and OpenAI had shown an ability to generate significant revenue from their latest models deployed for AI personal assistants. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk also subsequently responded, saying, “No crying in the casino,” weighing in on Tan’s concerns about speculative AI investments. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AVGO slipped to ‘extremely bearish’ at 24/100 — its lowest levels in nearly 18 months — from ‘bearish’ levels a day ago amid a 300% surge in 24-hour message volumes. Retail interest in the stock has been rising, with the ticker’s watcher base up 8% over the past three months. One user said, “The biggest problem with this stock is lack Catalysts from Broadcom, the last news was on Oct 13 for VMware HyperArmor. But nothing after it.”  Another user said, “Each time they beat earnings and revenue estimates. Yet here we are down 15% in that time frame.” A separate user said, “trash news! Still headed lower,” shortly after the Docomo agreement. Other traders were still looking for a bounce. Another user said, “when we sell off early into the session typically we see a nice reversal in overnight session into premarket.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. (CRWV) shares fell nearly 2% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. However, Cathie Wood's ARK Investment purchased 132,498 shares of the company on Monday despite the selloff. The asset manager’s ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought 102,280 CRWV shares on Monday for $6.3 million, according to its website. The firm also bought 30,218 shares of CRWV for $1.8 million through the ARK Next Generation Technology ETF (ARKW). The purchase comes as Wall Street and Main Street remain concerned about the company’s ballooning debt levels. CoreWeave reported $35.6 billion in total debt as of June 30, while its second-quarter net interest expense rose to $640 million from $267 million a year earlier. Research and advisory firm Gartner recently said in a report that artificial intelligence infrastructure investments are in danger as concerns over bloated AI capex mount. The firm said that as the commercial duopoly for primary frontier models consolidates around Anthropic and OpenAI, the cash flows to meet that massive computing asset base from neoclouds are not scaling proportionally with upfront costs. Meanwhile, major Wall Street analysts are also taking opposing stances on CoreWeave. MoffettNathanson and BNP Paribas lowered their price targets on CoreWeave, while Goldman Sachs took a more positive outlook. MoffettNathanson slashed CRWV stock’s target to $89 from $107 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares, citing its “staggering financial obligations.” BNP Paribas also cut its price target on CoreWeave to $117 from $169 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm said that it sees a continued deterioration in investor confidence amid its debt obligations. While higher financing costs could contain the company's ability to fund future growth, the shares are "seemingly discounting some liquidity concerns," the analyst reportedly said in a research note. However, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral’ and set a price target of $106, implying upside of more than 73% from its last close. The firm said ongoing volatility in the credit market raises questions about whether CoreWeave can finance its next phase of growth, and at what pace. However, Goldman also said the ongoing debate over demand for frontier vs. off-frontier intelligence, and CoreWeave's annual recurring revenue per megawatt and unlevered internal rate of return, are "biased to the upside" over the next 24 months because of tight supply. The analyst also said that CoreWeave is differentiated from other neoclouds. Last week, Dan Ives, Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director analyst, said in an interview that the recent sell-off was an overreaction, as the broader AI demand story remains intact. “I'm not saying there's not some issues in terms as rates go higher. But given the demand, given backlog, I think this is ultimately a false narrative,” he said, while also highlighting that the sharp drop has created an opportunity for investors. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for CRWV stock was ‘extremely bullish,’ even as message volumes surged 938% over 24 hours, according to platform data. EyePoint Pharmaceuticals (EYPT), CoreWeave (CRWV) and Eos Energy Enterprises (EOSE) hit fresh 52-week lows Monday as a failed drug trial, debt refinancing concerns, and weaker full-year revenue expectations weighed on the stocks. EyePoint stock crashed 85%, while CoreWeave and Eos Energy stocks dropped 0.4% and 0.5%, respectively. EyePoint Pharmaceuticals stock crashed to a record low of $0.4 after the company reported disappointing results from LUCIA, its second pivotal Phase 3 study of DURAVYU, an experimental treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The drug failed to show that it worked as well as aflibercept in protecting vision at Weeks 52 and 56, hurting its chances of approval for the eye condition. The setback prompted the company to lay off 53% of its workforce, with the restructuring expected to bring $30 million in annualized savings and incur about $9 million in severance expenses. EyePoint reported roughly $118 million in cash and equivalents as of Sept. 30 and plans to concentrate its remaining resources on Phase 3 studies of DURAVYU for diabetic macular edema (DME). However, on Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock flipped to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bearish’. CoreWeave stock fell to a new annual low of $59.25 as analysts cut price targets amid concerns about its debt obligations and reliance on external funding. BNP Paribas lowered its price target to $117 from $169 while retaining an ‘Outperform’ rating. MoffettNathanson cut its target to $89 from $107 and maintained a ‘Neutral’ rating. The analysts highlighted the potential consequences of weaker investor confidence and expensive financing. CoreWeave needs capital to expand its data center infrastructure and support growing demand for computing capacity. Higher borrowing costs and limited access to capital markets could complicate its expansion plans and weigh on shareholder returns. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Eos Energy Enterprises stock touched a two-year low of $1.72 despite reporting preliminary third-quarter (Q3) revenue of $82 million to $83 million, a sequential growth of 19% to 21%. However, investors focused on the company’s expectation that 2026 revenue would land in the lower half of its previously announced $300 million to $350 million range. The updated outlook follows an earlier reduction in the company's revenue forecast in August. Eos has recorded eight consecutive quarters of improving gross margins, but its margins remain deeply negative as it works to increase production and improve manufacturing efficiency at its Thorn Hill facility. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘bearish’. So far this year, EYPT, CRWV and EOSE stocks have declined between 14% and 97%. title: 3 Energy Dividend Stocks to Buy for More Than Oil Exposure - The Globe and Mail
content: Energy stocks can appeal to investors who want regular income, especially when markets are unsettled. Attacks on Saudi energy facilities and threats to tankers in the Middle East have increased uncertainty about oil supplies, giving investors another reason to look closely at how companies earn cash and pay dividends. ChevronCVX, Canadian Natural ResourcesCNQ and Kinder Morgan KMI,  are three dividend-paying energy stocks to buy. Their favorable ranks support the selection, while regular payouts add an income component to the investment case. Brent crude is around $110 a barrel, while U.S. crude is near $100. Attacks on Saudi energy facilities and ships near the Strait of Hormuz have raised fears of supply disruptions. Even if production continues, concerns that oil may not reach buyers can keep prices high. Saudi oil exports have nevertheless recovered. They reached a five-month high in August despite lower production. Later shipping estimates suggested crude exports were nearing pre-war levels. Delivering fuel remains a challenge. Restrictions on refined-fuel shipments and high shipping costs can squeeze refiners’ profits and raise costs for consumers. U.S. crude stockpiles also fell more than expected, adding to concerns about available supplies. Higher crude prices can help oil producers earn more, but they do not benefit every energy business equally. Expensive shipping and feedstock can raise costs elsewhere in the industry. That makes company cash flow a more useful starting point than a broad bet on oil. For dividend investors, the question is whether a company can cover its payout after funding its operations and necessary investment. Borrowing to maintain distributions would offer less comfort than paying them from cash the business generates. Kinder Morgan, Chevron and Canadian Natural Resources give investors different ways to approach energy income. Their ability to fund dividends after covering operating costs and investment needs matters most. Steady cash generation can help support those payments when energy prices weaken. Oil prices could stay high if attacks continue or shipping faces more disruptions. A recovery in exports or easing of the conflict could bring prices down. With both outcomes possible, investors should avoid relying on a single oil-price forecast. Established dividend payers can offer a more balanced approach. Their size, financial resources and ability to generate cash from different operations can help them navigate commodity-market swings while continuing to return capital to investors. Against this backdrop, Kinder Morgan, Chevron and Canadian Natural Resources offer three different ways to participate in the energy market while maintaining an income focus. Chevron: Chevron’s integrated business spans oil and gas exploration, production, refining and chemicals, providing multiple sources of cash flow across market cycles. Its broad geographic presence across the United States, the Asia-Pacific, Africa, the Middle East and South America, together with its scale and financial strength, supports free cash flow generation and continued shareholder returns. Chevron has maintained or raised its dividend for 90 years, underscoring a long track record of resilience. Its 3.1% yield exceeds both the sector and the S&P 500’s 1% average. A steady near-term earnings outlook, disciplined capital spending and continued efficiency gains should support the Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) company’s ability to sustain attractive shareholder payouts. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. Canadian Natural Resources: Canadian Natural Resources owns a large portfolio of long-life, low-decline assets producing light and heavy oil, bitumen, synthetic crude and natural gas. Its operations across Western Canada, the North Sea and offshore West Africa provide geographic and product diversification, while disciplined spending and a consistent focus on shareholder returns strengthen its appeal to income-oriented investors. The #1 Ranked company has increased its dividend for 26 consecutive years, supported by operational efficiency and consistent earnings performance. Its current quarterly dividend of 62.50 Canadian cents equates to a 3.3% yield, comfortably ahead of the Zacks Oil/Energy sector average of 2.5%. A strong balance sheet and efficient capital deployment reinforce the sustainability of its shareholder returns. Kinder Morgan: Kinder Morgan operates one of North America’s largest energy infrastructure networks, with 78,000 miles of pipelines and extensive storage assets. Its take-or-pay contracts across natural gas, refined products, crude oil and terminals generate relatively stable, fee-based cash flows, reducing sensitivity to short-term commodity-price swings and offering more defensive energy exposure during volatile market conditions. The Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) company expects a dividend increase in 2026, which would mark its ninth consecutive annual raise. Its current payout of 29.75 cents per quarter results in a 3.5% yield. With demand for natural gas and LNG infrastructure rising, Kinder Morgan’s asset base positions it well for continued cash flow durability. When oil firms, the output each field delivers fetches a stronger price, lifting the cash a large producer can generate without any change to the volume of barrels it brings to the surface. That leverage is central to the upstream business. The upstream arm finds and produces crude oil and natural gas across a spread of regions, feeding the barrels that anchor the group's earnings. The downstream arm refines that crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, while the marketing arm carries those fuels to end customers through a wide branded network. This integrated design lets the group capture value at several stages of the chain at after. Few threads have shaped the group's recent production as much as its position in the Permian basin, the vast shale region straddling the American Southwest that has become the engine of domestic oil growth. Those projects lengthen the group's production base and tie it to demand across many markets, broadening the mix beyond crude alone. The group has long carried a reputation for steady cash distributions to the holders of its stock, a feature that keeps it a staple of many broad market baskets. Alongside its core oil and gas base, the group has leaned into lower-carbon threads, from renewable fuels and hydrogen to carbon capture and storage ventures. As crude eased, refining margins stayed firm, a detail that carried weight for the downstream arm. The company manages a broad spread of oil and gas fields, pairing mature assets that generate steady cash with newer developments meant to add fresh barrels. The portfolio reaches across shale, deepwater and large conventional fields, giving the production book exposure to many geographies. A softer crude price sharpens focus on the cost of each barrel. The Permian, meanwhile, offers short-cycle shale wells that can be ramped or trimmed as prices move. The expansion of its stake in low-cost barrels has reshaped the company's production base, adding volumes that help offset decline elsewhere. Alongside these, the group carries assets spanning liquefied natural gas, offshore fields and conventional production, giving it reach across the full breadth of the oil and gas sector rather than exposure to any given region or grade of crude. Downstream and chemicals give the company levers beyond producing crude. Refining captures the spread between crude costs and fuel values, while chemicals turn hydrocarbons into resins and compounds for packaging, construction and consumer goods. Both arms move on rhythms that differ from the upstream business. With refining margins firm as crude eased, the downstream side provided a steadying counterweight. Chemicals follow their own cycle, tied to industrial activity and the cost of feedstock, and cheaper crude and gas can ease input costs for those plants. The wider energy sector moved together around the swing in crude. Oil and gas names tend to track the benchmark, rising when supply fears flare and easing when those fears fade. In that setting, the largest integrated names often serve as anchors. Their scale, diversified earnings and steady dividends give the market a reference point when crude churns. The energy cohort leaned on these heavyweight producers as traders weighed softer crude against firm refining margins, and the company stood among the most closely watched of them. The recent surge in crude traced to concern that global supply could tighten faster than new barrels could fill the gap. Geopolitics, disruptions and shifting plans among major exporters all feed that kind of unease, and prices tend to spike when scarcity dominates the conversation. The later easing reflected a calmer read on those same worries. For a group that both produces and refines, the swing is a lesson in balance. A sharp climb rewards production but pressures refining as feedstock costs rise.
